questions.stem: According to the review, what is the industry best-practice end state for a malware-infected machine, and what is the purpose of the 10-step procedure?

choices.text: Wipe and reimage from a known-good source; the 10-step process exists to rescue unbacked-up data before that wipe
Run one antivirus scan; the 10-step process is an alternative to scanning
Never wipe; the 10-step process permanently cleans without reinstalling
Replace the hardware; the 10-step process is for ordering parts

questions.explanation: Best practice is to nuke and reimage from a known-good source. The 10-step procedure exists to stabilize the system enough to rescue critical unbacked-up data before that wipe.
questions.trap: The 10-step process is not a substitute for reimaging; reimaging is still the guaranteed cleanup.

questions.stem: Immediately after verifying a malware infection (step 1), what is the critical next action (step 2)?

choices.text: Back up all files to a USB drive
Quarantine the system by disconnecting it from the network

questions.explanation: Step 2 is to quarantine the infected system - unplug Ethernet, disable Wi-Fi - so it cannot spread to the network.
questions.trap: You must NOT back up yet; backing up an infected machine just copies the malware. Also avoid USB drives at this stage.

questions.stem: Why does the procedure disable System Restore (step 3) during malware removal?

choices.text: To free up disk space for the antivirus
Because System Restore is not compatible with safe mode
Because malware often infects restore points, and disabling it deletes those contaminated points
To speed up the network connection

questions.explanation: Malware often hides in restore points. Disabling System Restore deletes the existing (possibly infected) points so you don't reintroduce the malware later.
questions.trap: It is not about disk space; it is about destroying contaminated restore points that could bring the malware back.

questions.stem: During remediation (steps 4-5), after attempting removal, what must you do immediately?

choices.text: Reconnect to the network to download games
Update the anti-malware engine and signature files

questions.explanation: After the first removal attempt, you must update the anti-malware software's engine and, most importantly, its latest signature files so it can recognize current threats.
questions.trap: Re-enabling System Restore comes much later (step 9), not during remediation.

questions.stem: Malware is preventing Windows from starting normally and blocking updates. Which advanced-scan technique should you try FIRST (step 6)?

choices.text: Boot into Safe Mode to load a minimal Windows that may stop the malware from running

questions.explanation: Safe Mode loads a minimal version of Windows, which can prevent the malware from running so you can scan and remove it.
questions.trap: Reimaging is the later best-practice end state; step 6 first tries Safe Mode (and, if that fails, WinPE).

questions.stem: If even Safe Mode cannot run, which command-line environment lets you access the file system from outside the corrupted OS to repair boot records or remove files?
questions.explanation: WinPE is a command-line environment that accesses the file system from outside the corrupted OS, used to repair boot records or manually remove files.
questions.trap: Task Manager only runs after Windows loads, so it cannot help when even Safe Mode fails.

questions.stem: Once the user's critical data is safely copied off (step 7), what is the recommended action?

choices.text: Leave the existing OS in place since data is saved
Reimage the drive from a known-clean image or do a fresh OS install
Reconnect to the network before cleaning

questions.explanation: After rescuing data, follow the real best practice: delete everything and reimage from a known-clean image or perform a fresh OS install - the only way to be 100% certain.
questions.trap: Leaving the infected OS in place risks residual malware; reimaging is the guaranteed cleanup.

questions.stem: In the final steps, after the system is clean you re-enable System Restore (step 9). What should you do right after enabling it?

choices.text: Immediately create a fresh, clean restore point

questions.explanation: After re-enabling System Restore, immediately create a fresh clean restore point as a known-good snapshot of the newly reimaged system.
questions.trap: Turning off Windows Update is the opposite of hardening; you want automatic security patches on.

questions.stem: What is the final step (step 10) of the malware removal process, described as most important for preventing a repeat incident?
questions.explanation: Step 10 is to educate the end user, since the user is the first line of defense against a repeat infection.
questions.trap: Quarantine and disabling System Restore are early steps; user education is the final, prevention-focused step.

questions.stem: During quarantine, which actions are explicitly warned against because they spread or preserve the infection?

choices.text: Using USB drives to move files and performing a backup of the infected system

questions.explanation: During quarantine you must not use USB drives to move files and must not back up the infected system - both spread or preserve the malware.
questions.trap: Disabling Wi-Fi and unplugging Ethernet is exactly what quarantine requires; that is correct, not warned against.
